source.title: The Promises and Pitfalls of Deep Kernel Learning
source.authors: Sebastian W. Ober; C. Rasmussen; Mark van der Wilk

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study compares batch sizes and reports their effects on held-out performance and train–test gaps, using DKL and neural-network models.
record.gate_note: The study also compares DKL with neural networks and reports overfitting, but those findings do not test the mapped versions about random-label memorization, width, architecture, optimizers, dropout, sharpness, or memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study measures batch-size sensitivity, but does not isolate V5's fixed-epoch comparison: CIFAR-10 runs hold gradient steps fixed, giving larger batches more epochs, and UTKFace follows the same procedure while measuring regression. Its feature-dimension sweep also does not test V2's widening of networks trained to convergence beyond zero training error. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors attribute much of DKL's practical success to stochastic minibatching rather than improved marginal likelihood, report stronger apparent stochastic regularization than in plain neural networks, and explain overfitting through excessive correlations encouraged by marginal-likelihood optimization. They conclude that fully Bayesian treatment can overcome this pathology; the empirical improvements are not uniform across all metrics.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines deep kernel learning and minibatch effects, rather than the original methods in the claim versions. It uses Adam and compares batch sizes in regression and image classification experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes DKL outcomes. On UTKFace and CIFAR-10, larger batches worsened some SVDKL held-out measures, while pNN changed little; on UTKFace, pSVDKL test RMSE improved even as test log likelihood worsened.

fits_no_version.finding: Without augmentation, increasing batch size worsens pSVDKL test log likelihood on UTKFace and CIFAR-10, improves UTKFace RMSE, and leaves CIFAR-10 accuracy unchanged at reported precision. CIFAR-10 uses equal gradient steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deep kernel learning can show metric-dependent batch-size sensitivity under equal-gradient-step training.

fits_no_version.finding: The tested larger batches leave pNN CIFAR-10 accuracy unchanged and do not significantly change its UTKFace performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch-size sensitivity differs between pretrained deterministic neural networks and jointly trained deep kernel models under the tested recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: With augmentation, pSVDKL test log likelihood worsens from -0.76 to -1.55 on UTKFace and from -0.64 to -0.84 on CIFAR-10 as batch size increases; CIFAR-10 accuracy remains 0.86.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation does not eliminate the tested deep kernel models' batch-size sensitivity in predictive log likelihood.

fits_no_version.finding: The feature-dimension sweep finds little performance change beyond a sufficient bottleneck size; CIFAR-10 NN and pNN train accuracy is 1.00 and test accuracy 0.79 at feature widths 10, 20, and 50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing a ResNet's final feature dimension beyond a sufficient bottleneck size need not improve test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Full-batch DKL can overfit more than a comparable deterministic neural network; stochastic minibatching generally mitigates this, and fully Bayesian inference improves several predictive measures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizing marginal likelihood over many kernel parameters does not reliably prevent overfitting; stochastic regularization and Bayesian inference can improve DKL performance.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2021)
record.problems: The study does not test random-label memorization or most mapped versions. Batch-size comparisons are limited to specified datasets and models; the authors note that batch-size effects require tuning. Table values are reported with standard errors over three runs for the image experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No additional mapped-version results were reported beyond the batch-size comparisons extracted. UCI batch-size findings are discussed qualitatively in the text and presented across multiple datasets in Figure 4 and Tables 7–11; detailed per-dataset outcomes are not included as rows because the batch-size comparison is not isolated there.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and their coexistence under the same recipe.
Widening networks trained to convergence beyond the width needed for zero training error; the final-feature bottleneck sweep does not establish this comparison.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size penalties under fixed epoch budgets, workload-dependent thresholds, and controlled tests of remedies for those penalties.
Effects of adding or removing dropout.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Accuracy effects of removing highly memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: All six rows contain valid reported measurements, but their V5 links and resulting verdicts should be removed. Fixed-gradient-step comparisons cannot determine the fixed-epoch effect. The additional augmentation and bottleneck-width findings fit no supplied version, so they do not require mapped-version missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons as stated in the version.
Adaptive optimizers are not compared; experiments use Adam.
Language models and fixed-epoch comparisons are not tested. The CIFAR-10 batch-size comparison uses the same number of gradient steps, and the paper does not establish a workload-dependent threshold.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures are not tested.
Removing memorized examples is not tested.
